extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close critical and interpretive analysis of Plato's Gorgias, extracting its main theses, rhetorical methods, and criteria for judging politicians, poets, and moral life. Aimed at understanding Plato's ethical and political standards and their relation to his other dialogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato's theory of punishment (vindictive vs corrective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato’s theory of punishment is partly vindictive, partly corrective: a few great criminals (chiefly tyrants) are reserved as examples, but for most men punishment is intended for their improvement; they are to suffer because they have sinned, like sick men who must go to the physician and be healed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: the analogy of disease and injustice is partial, and suffering may not improve but might worsen a person. Plato does not clearly distinguish suffering that improves from suffering that only punishes and deters, and he does not explain how punishment contributes to improvement. Compare with Christian doctrines of reward/punishment and avoid pressing the analogy too literally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in interpreting Plato's figurative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas must be given through something; the nature of the unseen mind can only be represented under figures derived from visible objects. These figures are imperfect and must not be construed too strictly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat metaphors or myths as literal statements of doctrine. Recognize that Plato sometimes reasons from figures as if they were realities due to the limited logical analysis of his age; avoid pressing his figures or asking questions beyond his intended horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main purpose of the Gorgias
rubrics_metrics.description: The main purpose is not to answer questions about a future world, but to place in antagonism the true and false life, and to contrast the judgments and opinions of men with judgment according to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the dialogue, subordinate topics (e.g., myths about the afterlife) should be read in service of this principal contrast between true and false living; avoid overemphasizing digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis of good and pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Good (permanent, objective) is opposed to pleasure (transient, subjective); in Gorgias and Phaedo, pleasure and good are distinctly opposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of unfairly opposing an objective account of the good to purely subjective happiness; consider that Plato's permanence-argument for good rests on assuming its objective character. If one focuses instead on subjective consciousness of happiness, that too may appear transient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts/sciences judged by relation to truth and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts or sciences, when pursued without any view to truth or the improvement of human life, are called flatteries — dependent upon the opinion of mankind and not true arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artistic or scientific practices by whether they seek truth and human improvement; if they aim merely at pleasing public opinion (flattery), they are morally and intellectually deficient in Plato’s account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inter-textual comparison with other dialogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare Gorgias to Republic, Philebus, Protagoras, Theaetetus etc.; similarities of spirit and language suggest relative dating and shared doctrines (e.g., education in Republic supplies what Gorgias suggests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing arguments and themes, situate them within Plato’s corpus: similar language and concepts may indicate common purpose or period; differences clarify distinctive emphases (e.g., Protagoras contrasts conception of happiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony and dramatic persona as modes of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato is a dramatic writer; the irony of Plato sometimes veils his idealism. The disguises Socrates assumes are like parables—half conceal, half reveal meaning. He may appear to jest when profoundly serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that the speaker's position equals Plato's; interpret ironic and dramatic passages with sensitivity to their rhetorical function. Expect mixture of jest and earnest—assess both form and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Thesis: doing injustice worse than suffering it
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a greater evil to do than to suffer injustice: moral evil is the only real evil; the righteous may suffer but are better than the wicked; consequences do not alter the morality of actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral actions by their intrinsic rightness/wrongness rather than by their consequences or rewards; resist consequentialist reduction of moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Thesis: suffering for wrongdoing as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to suffer for wrongdoing than not to suffer: hidden or delayed penalties can be educative; unpunished success removes reminders to correct oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat suffering (when proportionate) as potentially educational; consider how concealment of consequences leads to moral stagnation. Use examples (spoilt child, sovereign hidden from consequences) to illustrate the thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Thesis: weakness of will — 'we do not what we will, but what we wish'
rubrics_metrics.description: Good intentions or benevolent actions without wisdom are of no value; men often act against their own long-term interests because they fail to foresee consequences; 'virtue is knowledge' (virtue requires knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing moral agency, give weight to practical wisdom and foresight; distinguish mere good intention from knowledge-informed virtue. Recognize this as a partial truth bridging utilitarian and transcendental views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Thesis: 'to be and not to seem' — authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of life is to be, not to seem: individuals must seek inner truthfulness (acknowledge ignorance, correct evils, acquire firmness), not merely public reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character by inner consistency and private actions as well as public appearance; cultivate dispositions that enable independent judgment and moral firmness despite social pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for the true statesman
rubrics_metrics.description: The true statesman brings order out of disorder; first organizes then administers; is neither mere theorist nor dealer in expedients; conceives whole and parts together; is not of the world though he descends to it; pursues an ideal state aiming to unite freedom with order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific attributes: controls self before controlling others; knows mankind; has no private likes/dislikes; seeks long-term good (considers future generations); takes time for execution; educates followers until party ceases to be a party; adapts to times; has allies; enlightens public opinion; pursues permanent principles (better administration, education, reconciliation, security). Use these to judge political leadership against an ideal standard rather than mere popularity or short-term success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for the false politician
rubrics_metrics.description: The false politician is the serving-man of the state: he asks not what is true but what is the opinion of the world, not what is right but what is expedient; he values measures that will pass and seeks popularity; avoids persecution and uphill battles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify political actors who prioritize passing measures and popular approval over principle; such figures are judged negatively as lacking the statesmanlike qualities above.

rubrics_metrics.name: The poet's vocation: truth and ethical teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The true office of a poet or writer of fiction is not merely to give amusement but to teach: the poet clothes noblest truths with beauty, raises us through earthly things to the beyond, and invests familiar moral principles with new dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry and fiction by their ethical seriousness and ability to convey deep truths in beautiful form; distinguish works that merely stimulate emotions or amuse (mere pleasure) from those that aim at moral education and elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets and rhetoricians as parodies when opposed to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: When arts are pursued without truth or improvement they are 'parodies' of true arts; poets and rhetoricians who aim only at pleasure are imitators and minister to the weaker side of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge artistic and rhetorical productions by whether they serve the weaker side (pure pleasure/appeal) or aim at the good and truth; in the Republic such poets are expelled for being thrice removed from truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of dissent qualified: duty of the wise individual
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato asserts not an abstract right of toleration but the duty and right of the one wise and true man to dissent from the folly of the many; this is not a general endorsement of free expression but a model of prophetic dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing liberal toleration to Plato, be cautious: interpret his claim as authorization for a singular wise dissenter rather than a universal liberty to dissent. Expect consequent risks to the dissenter (e.g., fate of Socrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological note: avoid anachronistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato is not to be tried by a modern standard, but interpreted with reference to his place in the history of thought and the opinion of his time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Plato, situate judgments historically; account for differences in logical analysis and cultural presuppositions of his era; avoid pressing modern demands on ancient texts.
